**Gerard Salton and the SMART system — a dot product decides what you read (1961–1975)**

Gerard Salton began building SMART (System for the Mechanical Analysis and Retrieval of Text) at Harvard and developed it fully after moving to Cornell in 1965. His central move was to stop treating a document as prose and start treating it as a vector: one dimension for every word in the vocabulary, each entry a weighted count of how often that word appears. A user's query becomes a vector in the same space.

Ranking then becomes arithmetic you can already do. In "A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing" (Salton, Wong and Yang, Communications of the ACM, 1975), the score of a document against a query is the cosine of the angle between the two vectors — the dot product of the pair, divided by their two lengths. A document sharing the query's distinctive words points roughly the same way, so the dot product is large; a document with nothing in common sits near perpendicular and scores near zero. Salton's tf-idf weighting made common words count for less, so the alignment measured something meaningful.

SMART was the first system to use the model, and the arithmetic never left. Search engines built on Lucene still rank this way, and modern embedding search does too: the numbers in the vectors now come from a neural network rather than word counts, but the retrieval step is the same normalised dot product, run over millions of vectors at once.

That is why this lesson spends its time on one operation. Computing a dot product by hand, then taking the L2 norm to divide by, is exactly the pair of steps that decides which results a search box shows you.

studies.case_study:
**Bernard Widrow and Ted Hoff — gradient descent shipped inside a telephone modem (1960–2001)**

In 1960 at Stanford, Bernard Widrow and his doctoral student Marcian "Ted" Hoff built ADALINE, an ADAptive LINear Element. It predicted with a weighted sum of its inputs, compared that against the answer it should have given, and nudged its weights to shrink the error, one example at a time. The rule they wrote down is now called least mean squares, or LMS, and it is stochastic gradient descent on squared error: measure the error, take the gradient with respect to each weight, step the opposite way by a small amount.

The deployment is the surprising part. When the Franklin Institute awarded Widrow the 2001 Benjamin Franklin Medal in Engineering, the citation read "Pioneering work in Adaptive Signal Processing; LMS algorithm", and the Institute's account states that every high-speed modem contains an adaptive filter or automatic equaliser based on the Widrow–Hoff LMS algorithm. Telephone lines were never built to carry data; the equaliser learns each line's distortion while the call is live and corrects for it.

The step size mattered there exactly as it matters to you. Adaptive-filter theory gives an explicit upper bound on it: exceed the bound and the weights grow without limit instead of settling — the failure a modern training run shows as a loss that climbs or turns to `nan`. Set it far below and the filter is too slow to track a changing line.

So when this lesson hands you the update rule and then warns about the learning rate, that is not a beginner's footnote. It is the number engineers tuned on real hardware for decades before it acquired the name hyperparameter.

**Sally Clark — two probabilities multiplied together in a courtroom (1996–2003)**

Sally Clark, a solicitor, lost two infant sons: Christopher in December 1996 and Harry in January 1998. She was convicted of their murder in November 1999. The prosecution's most quoted evidence was a number: the paediatrician Sir Roy Meadow told the jury the chance of two cot deaths in a family like hers was 1 in 73 million — an estimate of roughly 1 in 8,500 for a single death, squared.

Two errors sit inside that sentence. Squaring assumes the deaths are independent, which they are not: siblings share genes and a household, so one natural infant death makes a second likelier. And taken at face value the figure is the probability of two natural deaths given innocence, not the probability of innocence given two deaths. Reading a conditional backwards is known as the prosecutor's fallacy; correcting it needs Bayes' theorem and a base rate, because double infant murder is also very rare. The comparison carries the information, not the number.

In October 2001 the Royal Statistical Society stated that there was no statistical basis for the figure, and expressed concern at the misuse of statistics in the courts. Her conviction was quashed in January 2003, after more than three years in prison — formally because a pathologist had withheld microbiology results pointing to natural causes, not because of the statistics. She never recovered, and died in 2007.

This lesson's worked example is the same arithmetic in a gentler setting: a rare disease, a test right 90% of the time, a positive result — and still only a 15% chance of illness. Ask of every probability: probability of what, given what?

**Morton Thiokol — a fitted relationship pushed past the edge of the data (1986–1989)**

On the night of 27 January 1986, engineers at Morton Thiokol, which built the Space Shuttle's solid rocket boosters, argued in a teleconference against launching Challenger the next morning in unusual cold. They suspected the rubber O-rings sealing the booster joints performed poorly when cold. The charts they sent showed the previous flights on which O-ring damage had been found — and only those. Flights with no damage were left off.

With that half of the evidence removed, the relationship all but disappeared. The Rogers Commission, the presidential inquiry, identified the deletion of the undamaged flights as a major flaw and redrew the chart with them added back, at which point the pattern is plain. The launch went ahead. Challenger broke apart after lift-off, killing seven people.

Three years later, statisticians Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley fitted a model to all 23 earlier flights in "Risk Analysis of the Space Shuttle: Pre-Challenger Prediction of Failure" (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989). Those flights had launched between 53°F and 81°F. Challenger launched at 31°F, colder than anything in the record, and their analysis put the chance of catastrophic field-joint O-ring failure there at at least 13%.

Two habits in this lesson are the defence. Fit on the data you have, including the rows that show nothing — dropping them is the same self-flattery as scoring a model on its training set. And respect where the data stops: a line fitted on houses of 1,000–2,000 sq ft says little about a mansion, and a model fitted between 53°F and 81°F said little about 31°F.

**Geoffrey Chang — two columns swapped, five papers retracted (2001–2006)**

Geoffrey Chang was a protein crystallographer at the Scripps Research Institute in California. In 2001 his group published in Science the first structure of MsbA, a complete ABC transporter — one of the membrane proteins that pump substances out of cells and matter greatly to drug resistance. It was read as a landmark, and more structures followed over the next four years.

In 2006 another laboratory published the structure of a related transporter, Sav1866, that looked nothing like Chang's. He went back through his pipeline and found the cause. As Science reported that December, under the headline "A Scientist's Nightmare: Software Problem Leads to Five Retractions", a homemade data-analysis program had flipped two columns of data, inverting the electron-density map from which the structures were built. Everything downstream had been derived from a mirror image.

Chang retracted five papers, published between 2001 and 2005 in Science, the Journal of Molecular Biology and PNAS. The program never raised an error. For five years it returned results that looked entirely plausible, and other laboratories designed experiments around them.

That is what an array bug looks like from the inside: no exception, no crash, only numbers that are wrong in a consistent way. The two tools in this lesson are the guard. Read `.shape` and print a few real values after every transformation rather than trusting that an operation did what you meant. And commit the exact code beside the result it produced, so that when a number is later questioned you can rerun the thing that made it.
